# Introduction

This project describes Japan's postwar growth experience and decomposes its
output growth into the contributions of capital, labor, and total factor
productivity (TFP). The aggregate analysis follows the Solow growth accounting
framework taught in class, using the Penn World Table (PWT 11.0). The
industry-flavored extension uses the EU KLEMS growth accounts to look at the
composition of capital and the role of labor quality after 1995.

Japan is a natural case for growth accounting because its growth rate changed so
dramatically over time. The economy moved through a postwar miracle, a slowdown
after the oil shocks, an asset bubble, a long stagnation known as the Lost
Decade, and a modest recovery under Abenomics. The central question this report
asks is simple: when growth slowed, which input slowed with it? The answer turns
out to be mostly TFP, and the decomposition lets us say that precisely.

# Data

```{r load-pwt}
pwt <- read_excel("pwt110.xlsx", sheet = "Data")

jpn_pwt <- pwt %>%
  filter(countrycode == "JPN") %>%
  select(country, countrycode, year,
         rgdpna, rnna, rkna, emp, avh, hc, labsh, rtfpna, delta) %>%
  arrange(year)
```

```{r load-klems}
get_klems <- function(path, sheet, var_name, total_code = "TOT") {
  read_excel(path, sheet = sheet) %>%
    filter(nace_r2_code == total_code) %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = matches("^[0-9]{4}$"),
                 names_to = "year", values_to = var_name) %>%
    mutate(year = as.integer(year)) %>%
    select(year, all_of(var_name))
}

f <- "JP_growth accounts.xlsx"

jpn_klems <- list(
  get_klems(f, "VA_G",          "VA_G"),
  get_klems(f, "VAConTFP",      "VAConTFP"),
  get_klems(f, "VAConH",        "VAConH"),
  get_klems(f, "VAConLC",       "VAConLC"),
  get_klems(f, "VAConTangICT",  "VAConTangICT"),
  get_klems(f, "VAConTangNICT", "VAConTangNICT"),
  get_klems(f, "VAConIntang",   "VAConIntang")
) %>%
  Reduce(function(a, b) full_join(a, b, by = "year"), .) %>%
  arrange(year)
```

The aggregate analysis uses PWT 11.0, which covers Japan from 1950 to 2023 at
the country level. Following the lecture (slides 35 and 36), the key variables
are real GDP (`rgdpna`), capital services (`rkna`), persons engaged (`emp`), and
the labor share (`labsh`). The extension uses the EU KLEMS growth accounts for
Japan, which cover 1995 to 2021 and provide pre-computed contributions of hours,
labor quality, three types of capital, and TFP.

Three measurement points shape how the results should be read, and they are
revisited in Section 4.4. First, in PWT 11.0 capital services (`rkna`) and the
TFP index (`rtfpna`) are missing for 1950 to 1953, so any term that uses them
effectively begins in 1954. Second, the labor share is held constant at about
0.51 until 1970 before it starts to move, so the earliest decomposition leans on
an assumed share. Third, because this release is PWT 11.0 while the lecture table
used PWT 10.0, the numbers differ somewhat even though the pattern does not.

# Growth Facts

## Real GDP and GDP per worker

```{r growth-facts-compute}
facts <- jpn_pwt %>%
  arrange(year) %>%
  mutate(
    gdp_pw   = rgdpna / emp,
    g_gdp    = (rgdpna / lag(rgdpna) - 1) * 100,
    g_gdp_pw = (gdp_pw / lag(gdp_pw) - 1) * 100
  )
```

```{r fig-gdp-growth, fig.cap="Annual growth of real GDP and real GDP per worker, Japan (PWT 11.0)."}
facts %>%
  select(year, g_gdp, g_gdp_pw) %>%
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "series", values_to = "growth") %>%
  mutate(series = recode(series,
                         g_gdp = "Real GDP",
                         g_gdp_pw = "Real GDP per worker")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, growth, color = series)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Annual growth (%)", color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The figure shows the central fact of the Japanese economy. Growth rates that
were extraordinarily high in the 1950s and 1960s, frequently above eight
percent and peaking near thirteen percent in 1960, fall sharply after the early
1970s and settle close to zero from the 1990s onward. Real GDP per worker tracks
the headline series closely until the 1990s, then sits visibly below it. That
gap is the first clue to the recent slowdown: total GDP and per-worker GDP
diverge because the workforce stops growing and later shrinks, so part of the
later weakness is demographic rather than productivity-based. The deep troughs
at 2009 and 2020 mark the global financial crisis and the pandemic.

## The labor income share

```{r fig-labsh, fig.cap="Labor compensation share in GDP, Japan (PWT 11.0)."}
jpn_pwt %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, labsh)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7, color = "#1f4e79") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Labor share of GDP")
```

The labor share is reported as flat at about 0.508 until 1970, then rises
quickly to around 0.62 by the mid-1970s, drifts down through the 1990s and
2000s, and recovers after 2010. The sharp step around 1970 should be read with
care. It reflects how PWT constructs the early series rather than a sudden real
shift in how income was split between workers and capital, and it matters
because growth accounting weights each input by its income share. Setting the
artificial step aside, the broad picture is consistent with the balanced growth
path of the Solow model and with the Kaldor facts discussed in class: the share
stays within a fairly narrow band over the long run.

## Economic events behind the patterns

The growth facts line up with a familiar sequence of events. The years to 1973
are the postwar miracle, supported by high savings, heavy investment, and the
movement of workers out of agriculture into manufacturing. The 1973 and 1979 oil
shocks hit an energy-importing economy hard and end the miracle. The 1985 Plaza
Accord and the loose monetary policy that followed inflated an asset bubble in
the late 1980s. Its collapse in 1991 opens the Lost Decade, which lingers through
the deflation of the 2000s and the global financial crisis of 2008 and 2009. The
Abenomics program from 2013 combines aggressive monetary easing, fiscal
stimulus, and structural reform. The 2020 pandemic produces a sharp contraction
and rebound at the very end of the sample.

# Growth Accounting

## Method

We use the Solow decomposition in the notation of the lecture. Output growth is
split into the contribution of capital, the contribution of labor, and a
residual that measures TFP growth:
$$
\frac{\Delta Y_t}{Y_t}
= \bar{s}^{K}_{t}\,\frac{\Delta K_t}{K_t}
+ \bar{s}^{L}_{t}\,\frac{\Delta L_t}{L_t}
+ \frac{\Delta A_t}{A_t}.
$$
Growth rates are simple period-over-period changes, for example
$\Delta Y_t / Y_t = (Y_t - Y_{t-1})/Y_{t-1}$. The factor shares are time
averages, $\bar{s}^{L}_{t} = (s^{L}_{t} + s^{L}_{t-1})/2$, and under constant
returns with competitive pricing the capital share is
$\bar{s}^{K}_{t} = 1 - \bar{s}^{L}_{t}$. Following the lecture, output is
`rgdpna`, capital is capital services `rkna`, labor is persons engaged `emp`, and
the labor share is `labsh`. The TFP term is the Solow residual, the part of
output growth left unexplained by measured capital and labor.

```{r ga-compute}
ga <- jpn_pwt %>%
  arrange(year) %>%
  mutate(
    g_Y    = rgdpna / lag(rgdpna) - 1,
    g_K    = rkna   / lag(rkna)   - 1,
    g_L    = emp    / lag(emp)    - 1,
    sL_bar = (labsh + lag(labsh)) / 2,
    sK_bar = 1 - sL_bar,
    contrib_K = sK_bar * g_K,
    contrib_L = sL_bar * g_L,
    tfp       = g_Y - contrib_K - contrib_L
  )
```

## Year-by-year decomposition

```{r fig-decomp, fig.cap="Contributions to annual real GDP growth: capital, labor, and TFP. Bars sum to output growth (the black line)."}
ga %>%
  filter(year >= 1955) %>%
  select(year, TFP = tfp, Capital = contrib_K, Labor = contrib_L, g_Y) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(TFP, Capital, Labor),
               names_to = "component", values_to = "contribution") %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_col(aes(year, contribution * 100, fill = component), width = 0.9) +
  geom_line(aes(year, g_Y * 100), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(TFP = "#c44e52",
                               Capital = "#4c72b0",
                               Labor = "#55a868")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Contribution to GDP growth (%)", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The figure makes the regime change visible. In the early decades all three
components are large and positive, with capital doing the heaviest lifting. After
1973 the bars shrink across the board. During the Lost Decade the TFP bars turn
negative in several years, and what little growth remains is held up by capital.
In the most recent years the bars are small in every color, which is the picture
of a low-growth economy in which no single input is driving expansion.

## Sub-period averages

```{r ga-subperiod}
ga <- ga %>%
  mutate(period = case_when(
    year > 1950 & year <= 1973 ~ "1950-1973",
    year > 1973 & year <= 1983 ~ "1973-1983",
    year > 1983 & year <= 1991 ~ "1983-1991",
    year > 1991 & year <= 2000 ~ "1991-2000",
    year > 2000 & year <= 2010 ~ "2000-2010",
    year > 2010 & year <= 2019 ~ "2010-2019",
    year > 2019 & year <= 2023 ~ "2019-2023",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ))

subperiod_tab <- ga %>%
  filter(!is.na(period)) %>%
  group_by(Period = period) %>%
  summarise(
    `Output growth` = mean(g_Y,       na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    `TFP`           = mean(tfp,       na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    `Capital`       = mean(contrib_K, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    `Labor`         = mean(contrib_L, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r tab-subperiod}
kable(subperiod_tab, digits = 2, booktabs = TRUE,
      caption = "Growth accounting for Japan, sub-period averages. Average annual growth rate (\\%). Source: PWT 11.0.")
```

This table is the heart of the project, and the story reads cleanly down the
rows. The miracle period (1950 to 1973) combines a very large capital
contribution of 5.42 points with strong TFP growth of 2.73, together producing
output growth near nine percent. In the oil-shock decade (1973 to 1983) output
growth more than halves to 3.50, and the fall is mostly in TFP, which collapses
from 2.73 to 0.39 while capital stays substantial at 2.73. The bubble years
(1983 to 1991) bring a partial TFP recovery to 1.67.

The Lost Decade (1991 to 2000) is the pivotal row. TFP turns negative at minus
0.66, so the only thing keeping output growth positive at 1.05 is residual
capital accumulation of 1.74. In other words, firms kept investing into an
economy whose productivity was actually falling. The 2000s (2000 to 2010)
flatten everything: output growth of just 0.60, near-zero TFP, and a labor
contribution that turns negative at minus 0.20 as the working-age population
begins to shrink. The Abenomics years (2010 to 2019) show labor turning positive
again at 0.40, helped by rising participation among women and older workers,
while the capital contribution nearly disappears. The final pandemic sub-period
(2019 to 2023), which the lecture table does not cover, shows the sharp 2020
contraction with negative TFP of minus 0.24.

The single clearest message is that Japan's great slowdown is primarily a TFP
story. The capital contribution declines gradually and predictably as the
capital-to-output ratio matures, but it is the swing in TFP, from plus 2.73 in
the miracle to minus 0.66 in the Lost Decade, that accounts for most of the
collapse in growth.

## Data limitations

Two limitations are worth noting. First, PWT 11.0 does not report capital
services (`rkna`) or the TFP index (`rtfpna`) before 1954, so the capital and
TFP averages for the 1950 to 1973 sub-period are computed from 1954 onward.
This is why the components in that row do not sum exactly to output growth: the
three terms are averaged over slightly different windows. Every other row
reconciles to the second decimal.

Second, the labor share is held constant at about 0.51 until 1970 in this
release, so the earliest decomposition relies on an assumed share rather than
measured data. The split between capital and labor in the first sub-period
should therefore be read as indicative rather than precise.

# Additional Analysis: Basic versus Extended TFP

## Idea

The decomposition above treats labor as a simple headcount and capital as a
single index. The Jorgenson and Griliches measurement program, discussed in
class, argues that much of what we call TFP is really unmeasured improvement in
input quality. When we account for the rising education of workers and the shift
toward more productive types of capital, the measured residual should shrink.

We compare two residuals. The basic residual uses the capital stock (`rnna`) and
headcount labor (`emp`). The extended residual is PWT's own `rtfpna`, which
already quality-adjusts labor by hours and human capital and uses capital
services. The gap between them is the part of measured TFP that is actually
input quality.

```{r basic-extended-compute}
sens <- jpn_pwt %>%
  arrange(year) %>%
  mutate(
    g_Y       = rgdpna / lag(rgdpna) - 1,
    g_Kstock  = rnna   / lag(rnna)   - 1,
    g_Lhead   = emp    / lag(emp)    - 1,
    sL_bar    = (labsh + lag(labsh)) / 2,
    sK_bar    = 1 - sL_bar,
    tfp_basic = g_Y - sK_bar * g_Kstock - sL_bar * g_Lhead,
    tfp_ext   = rtfpna / lag(rtfpna) - 1
  ) %>%
  mutate(period = case_when(
    year > 1950 & year <= 1973 ~ "1950-1973",
    year > 1973 & year <= 1983 ~ "1973-1983",
    year > 1983 & year <= 1991 ~ "1983-1991",
    year > 1991 & year <= 2000 ~ "1991-2000",
    year > 2000 & year <= 2010 ~ "2000-2010",
    year > 2010 & year <= 2019 ~ "2010-2019",
    year > 2019 & year <= 2023 ~ "2019-2023",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ))

sens_tab <- sens %>%
  filter(!is.na(period)) %>%
  group_by(Period = period) %>%
  summarise(
    `Basic TFP`    = mean(tfp_basic, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    `Extended TFP` = mean(tfp_ext,   na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(`Difference` = `Basic TFP` - `Extended TFP`)
```

```{r tab-basic-extended}
kable(sens_tab, digits = 2, booktabs = TRUE,
      caption = "Basic versus extended TFP growth for Japan. Average annual growth rate (\\%). The difference is the part of measured TFP attributable to input quality. Source: PWT 11.0.")
```

The extended residual is smaller than the basic one in every sub-period, which
is exactly the Jorgenson and Griliches result: once we credit the rising quality
of labor and capital, less of growth looks like pure technical change. The
difference is largest in the miracle period at 1.40 points, when education was
expanding fast and the capital stock was being upgraded rapidly, and it narrows
to near zero in the recent decades as those quality gains slow. This is a clean
demonstration that measured TFP is, in part, a measure of our ignorance about
input quality.

# Additional Analysis: Capital Composition (EU KLEMS)

## Idea

PWT treats capital as one aggregate. EU KLEMS splits the capital contribution
into three groups: information and communication technology (ICT), other
tangible capital (non-ICT), and intangible capital such as software, research
and development, and organizational capital. This lets us see how the
composition of investment changed over Japan's recent decades.

```{r fig-klems-capital, fig.cap="EU KLEMS contributions to value-added growth by capital type, labor quality, and TFP, Japan 1995-2021."}
jpn_klems %>%
  select(year,
         `Labor quality` = VAConLC,
         `ICT capital` = VAConTangICT,
         `Non-ICT capital` = VAConTangNICT,
         `Intangible capital` = VAConIntang,
         `TFP` = VAConTFP) %>%
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "component", values_to = "contribution") %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, contribution, fill = component)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "ICT capital"        = "#4c72b0",
    "Non-ICT capital"    = "#8da0cb",
    "Intangible capital" = "#c49a3f",
    "Labor quality"      = "#55a868",
    "TFP"                = "#c44e52"
  )) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Contribution to value-added growth (%)", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The EU KLEMS picture confirms and enriches the PWT story for the post-1995
period. Intangible capital makes a small but steady positive contribution
throughout, which a stock-only measure like PWT would miss entirely, and it is
one of the few inputs that never turns negative. The TFP contribution is
volatile and often negative around the Lost Decade and the financial crisis,
which matches the negative residual found in the aggregate analysis and is a
useful cross-check between two independent datasets. Labor quality keeps adding
to growth even as the headcount stagnates, reflecting the continued upgrading of
Japan's workforce through education and experience.

# Conclusion

Japan's growth history is a story of switching engines. In the miracle decades,
capital accumulation and strong TFP growth drove output up at rates close to ten
percent. The oil shocks ended the easy catch-up gains, and the bursting of the
asset bubble in 1991 opened a long stagnation in which TFP growth turned
negative and capital accumulation was the only thing holding growth above zero.
The recent period shows a modest TFP recovery fighting against a shrinking
workforce.

The growth accounting exercise makes these transitions precise. Reproducing the
lecture table with the newest PWT data confirms the pattern, and the slowdown is
shown to be primarily a TFP phenomenon rather than a capital or labor one. The
basic-versus-extended comparison shows that a meaningful share of measured TFP is
really input quality, exactly as the Jorgenson and Griliches program predicts.
The EU KLEMS extension adds the role of intangible capital and labor quality that
an aggregate dataset cannot see, and independently reproduces the negative-TFP
signature of the Lost Decade.

Jorgenson, D. W., and Griliches, Z. (1967). The Explanation of Productivity
